summary: Defines a GMPLS lambda label format for the flexi-grid in LSC routers, which can describe slices of spectrum of different widths. It updates RFCs 3471 and 6205.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a name tag for a slice of light that can be wider or narrower.

questions: what is the flexi-grid label format
how are flexi-grid wavelengths identified in gmpls
what does the m field mean in a flexi-grid label
what is a compound label in gmpls
subtitle: A 64-bit GMPLS label that names a slice of optical spectrum of any width on the flexi-grid.

tldr.problem: GMPLS lambda labels could only pick entries from fixed wavelength grids, but the ITU-T flexi-grid lets a channel take a variable-width slice of spectrum.
tldr.mechanism: A new 64-bit label keeps the fixed-grid fields (Grid, C.S., Identifier, n) and adds a 16-bit m field for slot width, with Grid value 3 and C.S. value 5. Several labels can be concatenated into a compound label.
tldr.outcome: LSC routers can signal flexi-grid slots in a standard way; the RFC updates RFC 3471 and RFC 6205 and leaves the optical data plane to ITU-T.

today: RFC 7699 is a Proposed Standard. It updates RFC 3471 and RFC 6205, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a New Label
sections.content:
GMPLS extends MPLS beyond packet switching to other interface types, including Lambda Switch Capable (LSC) interfaces that switch wavelengths. RFC 3471 says wavelength labels only have significance between two neighbors, and RFC 6205 then defined a lambda label format with global meaning for the DWDM and CWDM grids.

The ITU-T has since defined a flexi-grid: a fine-granularity grid from which channels can be chosen as arbitrarily assigned pieces of spectrum, each with a width suited to its bit rate and modulation. This RFC continues the theme of RFC 6205 by defining a label for it. It relies on ITU-T G.694.1 for the optical data plane and makes no changes to the ITU-T's work.
sections.plainLanguage: Old name tags only worked for boxes of one size. The shelf now allows boxes of different widths, so we need a new kind of tag.

sections.title: How the Flexi-Grid Works
sections.content:
A flexi-grid data channel is formed from an abstract grid anchored at 193.1 THz, selected on a channel spacing of 6.25 GHz, with a variable slot width measured in units of 12.5 GHz. Allocations can be made from anywhere in the spectrum as long as they do not overlap.

Equipment need not support every position or width. G.694.1 gives the example of an application using only even values of the position number and only slot widths that are multiples of 25 GHz.

The fixed-grid label of RFC 6205 has four fields: Grid, C.S. (channel spacing), Identifier (a locally scoped integer to tell lasers apart) and n (a two's-complement integer used to compute frequency). Frequency in THz is 193.1 plus n times the frequency granularity, which is 0.00625 THz for the flexible grid.
sections.plainLanguage: Picture a ruler with tiny marks. You pick a starting mark and how many wide blocks you want, as long as nobody else is using that part.

sections.title: The Flexi-Grid Label
sections.content:
The flexi-grid label is 64 bits long. Its first 32 bits follow the fixed-grid layout (Grid, C.S., Identifier, n) and the second 32 bits hold m and a Reserved field.

This RFC adds Grid value 3 ("ITU-T Flex") and C.S. value 5 (6.25 GHz). For the flexible grid, C.S. gives the nominal central frequency granularity rather than a fixed spacing between channels. Identifier and n keep their RFC 6205 meanings.

The 16-bit integer m gives the slot width: slot width in GHz is 12.5 times m. Reserved MUST be set to zero on transmission and SHOULD be ignored on receipt.

An implementation using this label MUST follow the procedures of RFC 3473 and of RFC 3471 as updated by RFC 6205, and MUST set Grid to 3, C.S. to 5, Identifier to the local laser identifier, n by the frequency formula and m by the width formula. Because the label format is known a priori, every node on the path must expect to use it.
sections.plainLanguage: The tag has a place for the kind of ruler, how fine its marks are, which laser, where your spot starts (n) and how wide it is (m).

sections.title: Bandwidth and Compound Labels
sections.content:
In a flexi-grid system the label also determines the slot width and so the bandwidth an LSP supports. The m parameter is therefore both part of the label and part of the bandwidth. In GMPLS signaling bandwidth is requested in the SENDER_TSPEC object and confirmed in FLOWSPEC, and m also appears in the flexi-grid Tspec and Flowspec defined in a separate draft.

To signal an LSP over several slots, a compound label is built by concatenating 64-bit flexi-grid labels in the LABEL object. The number of labels, r, follows from the object length, which is 4 + 8r; with r equal to 1 the result is the single label. Component labels MUST be in increasing order of n.

Each component must show Grid 3 and the same C.S. value; Identifier may point to different equipment. At the time of writing G.694.1 only supports groups of adjacent slots of identical width in increasing frequency order, and the mechanism MUST NOT be used for other groupings until the ITU-T defines them. Nothing about how the signal is encoded across the slots may be inferred from the label.
sections.plainLanguage: If you need more room than one spot gives, you can staple several tags together, in order from left to right. Today the spots have to sit side by side and be the same width.

sections.title: Compatibility and Management
sections.content:
GMPLS assumes both ends of a link know which label types are in use, since label objects carry no type identifier. A legacy node that receives a flexi-grid label will process it as a type it knows, with a potentially poor outcome, so it should not be sent one. Flexi-grid labels that merely pass through a legacy node, for example in a Record Route Object, have no impact beyond management effects.

No new management elements are introduced. A system expecting a 32-bit lambda label can read the first 32 bits as in RFC 6205 but will not recognize the new Grid value and may give up parsing the message. The RFC suggests a two-step management upgrade: first handle the 64-bit length, possibly showing the label as an opaque quantity or reading the first 32 bits as before; then parse flexi-grid labels field by field.
sections.plainLanguage: Old equipment only knows the small tags. If it is handed the new tag it may be confused, so only give new tags to equipment that expects them.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
The RFC states that, as RFC 6205 noted for its own new label encoding, defining a new label encoding adds no new security considerations beyond those of RFC 3471 and RFC 3473. It points to the MPLS/GMPLS security framework in RFC 5920 for general discussion.

IANA has added one entry to the Grid subregistry (value 3, "ITU-T Flex") and one to the DWDM Channel Spacing subregistry (value 5, 6.25 GHz), both in the GMPLS Signaling Parameters registry.
sections.plainLanguage: A new kind of name tag does not create new safety problems of its own. The new numbers were added to the official list.

sections.title: Worked Example
sections.content:
The appendix encodes a hop of an optical LSP with a slot centred at 193.05 THz, a granularity of 6.25 GHz and a slot width of 50 GHz.

Grid is 3 and C.S. is 5. Solving 193.05 = 193.1 + n * 0.00625 gives n = -8. Solving 50 = 12.5 * m gives m = 4. Identifier is the local value for the laser in use.
sections.plainLanguage: To rent a 50-wide spot, you say each block is 12.5 wide, so you want 4 blocks. Your start point is a little left of the middle mark, which is the minus sign.

fields.name: C.S.
fields.desc: Nominal central frequency granularity; 5 means 6.25 GHz.

fields.name: Identifier
fields.desc: Local identifier of the laser in use.

fields.name: n
fields.desc: Two's-complement integer that sets the central frequency.

fields.name: m
fields.desc: Slot width in units of 12.5 GHz.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Set to zero on send, ignored on receipt.
